The next two years will be critical in determining whether this administration can deliver on its promises and have a long-term positive impact on the country . <p> T he worn green cover of a Nigerian passport , for many , represents a beacon of hope -- a key to global opportunities , trade , and even refuge . Yet , for a growing number of Nigerian citizens , that very document has become a gateway not to a foreign land , but to a bewildering cycle of denial , detention , and a humiliating , often inaccurate , label : " deportee . " This pervasive predicament , quietly endured by countless travelers , exposes a darker underbelly of international borders , where hopeful journeys frequently end in confined spaces and dashed dreams . As one exasperated business traveler lamented , the process feels like " borderline exploitation , " with a hidden financial and emotional cost no one dares to articulate . While authorities may legally apply the ' deportee ' tag , legal and Nigerian immigration experts argue that the classification itself is often a cruel misnomer , blurring the lines between a genuine expulsion and a simple , yet devastating , denial of entry . TOMI FALADE 's investigation delves into the perplexing reality faced by Nigerian passport holders , scrutinising the reasons behind these frequent rejections , the grim realities of their subsequent detentions , and the broader , uncomfortable questions about global perceptions and national responsibility . <p> Picture this : two Nigerian businessmen , planning new expansion , embarked on a business-cum-tourist trip to Singapore joined by three of their Canadian passport-carrying colleagues . At the point of entry , only Nigerians were denied entry at the Singapore Changi Airport . Not only were they denied , but they were held in an airport detention room for five days with restricted phone access , even after their Singaporean counterparts came to vouch for their authenticity . Inspite of no backing evidence -- just a lack of immediate available seats on the aircraft -- they were tagged " deportees " and handed back to the airline they came with for return to Nigeria five days after their arrival , forfeiting non-refundable hotel payments . <p> To add insult to injury , despite having return tickets , the airline demanded an additional N304,000 before their passports could be returned . <p> According to the 40-year-old Nigerian man , one of the duo who suffered the ordeal , " It is borderline exploitation . I believe many of these countries are using Nigeria to drum up funds . I believe it is a form of racketeering , because why give me a visa you do not plan to honour just because I carry a green passport . <p> " It 's undeniable that some Nigerians have committed reprehensible acts abroad , but I believe if a nation harbours prejudice against us , they should state it openly : ' Nigerians are not welcome . ' Countries should be forthright enough to declare Nigeria unwelcome . Such clarity would prevent honest Nigerians from embarking on futile journeys , and any Nigerian who subsequently tries to enter could then be classified as a criminal . But to merely sight my green passport and without specific justification deny me entry -- that is simply inhumane and an affront to basic human dignity . <p> " We pay exorbitant amounts to be denied visas . The few that are then granted visas will still then be denied entry thereby forfeiting huge amount of money . I spent a little over N10 million on this trip , yet no one is talking about it . They make the process such that any money spent is gone forever . It is unfair . No one is talking about these hidden cost of denied entries even when you get back to Nigeria . " <p> An official at the Nigerian Immigration Service ( NIS ) , who preferred anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter , shed light on the complexities . <p> " Many Nigerians get to these countries , and the country refuses to accept them and sends them back home . These are the ones that have already been appraised , maybe questioned or whatever , and are then sent back , " the official explained . <p> " As a returnee , you are supposed to be sent back on the same flight ... But if , for any reason , you enter the country and they take you to a detention center or elsewhere , then it 's a different case . You might not even know the real reason ... If you stay there one week , two weeks , or three weeks , then it 's considered deportation . <p> " On the Nigerian end the tag deportee depends on what the other country is tagging you as . " The official confirmed that if a foreign country 's paperwork states " deported , " NIS adheres to that , especially in cases involving security issues . " As a deportee , we have the right to seize your passport for investigation , " the official added , noting that while passengers with return tickets should n't typically pay extra , airlines are often fined by destination countries ( and by Nigeria for inadmissible passengers , at $2,000 ) , a cost often " transferred those charges to the passenger , which is fair . " <p> However , the NIS official pointed to a deeper issue regarding Nigeria 's image . While acknowledging NIS 's efforts to improve the perception of the Nigerian passport , they lamented , " But we Nigerians ourselves are not helping matters . If you 're trying from one side , someone else is sabotaging it from the other side . That 's the challenge we face . " <p> Citing a former minister whose passport was briefly seized in Germany , the official stressed , " It 's what our people are doing . While some people are trying to improve the perception of Nigerians abroad , others are doing things that make them suspect all of us . " They concluded by urging collective responsibility : " If you are good , and I am good , and we represent the country well , we wo n't have any problems . But when one out of every three , or even two out of three , have bad records or bad intentions , that 's the real problem . " <p> A Lagos-based lawyer , Barrister Adetunji Adegboyega offered a legal perspective , emphasising that " every country reserve the rights to admit , to accept anybody to come into their country . " He clarified that " the fact that one even has a visa , is not a guarantee that you will not be denied entry into the country . It 's still their prerogative . " <p> Adegboyega noted that detention is n't universal but often occurs when authorities " discover that maybe some there 's some fraudulent documentation in the process of the that led to the obtaining of the visa . " Crucially , he affirmed , " the moment you are not allowed entry into that country , it means or it states that you are deported " He further elaborated that if a country imposes fees for passport retrieval or other charges , " There 's nothing anybody can do in that regard . " <p> Adegboyega did not shy away from addressing the pervasive negative stereotypes . Recounting a personal experience in the US where he was jokingly called " the Nigerian Prince , " he stated , " Almost everywhere it 's shameful , it 's bad ... it 's a negative tag that we have put on ourselves . " <p> However , he balanced this by stressing that while individual responsibility is key , the government has a crucial role to play in image management . " A lot of these things is propaganda , " he asserted , citing America 's carefully curated image that often differs from reality on the ground . " Why are we also not doing the same thing ? Those are the part that the government also have to play to make sure that they present the right and positive image of the country . " <p> He concluded by emphasising that the bad actors are " very minute , " yet their actions cast a wide , damaging shadow , underscoring the need for both citizens and the nation to work collectively to project a positive image . <p> The green passport , therefore , remains a complex symbol : a testament to Nigerian identity , yet increasingly a marker of a global battle for dignity and fair treatment . But it is evident that until nations confront their biases and Nigeria actively reclaims its narrative , the " Green Passport Predicament " will continue to cast a long , humiliating shadow over the aspirations of countless Nigerians seeking their place in the world . <p> A heartbreaking crisis has continued to unfold in Benue State , once known as the nation 's " Food Basket . " This is a story of rising violence , displacement , and loss , with communities and local governments devastated by relentless attacks and a sense of abandonment . ROLAND OGBONNAYA chronicles the devastating impact on the Benue people , using the voices of grieving residents , frustrated leaders , and concerned observers to paint a vivid picture of a land where the promise of prosperity has been replaced by the stark reality of fear , hunger , and death . <p> The air in Aondoana , Gw ? er-West Local Government Area , Benue State , was heavy with sadness . Children 's Day , May 27th , 2025 , was supposed to be a day of celebration , devoted to the joy and innocence of childhood . Instead of laughter and games , the earth was turned , not for planting , but for bury ? ing the dead . <p> Among the rows of freshly dug graves lay a tiny coffin . Inside , the lifeless body of a two-year-old child , a victim of the most recent round of brutal attacks by alleged Fulani herd ? ers . This child , who should have been celebrating his special day , was instead laid to rest alongside the other thirteen victims of the May 25th attack on Aon ? doana . <p> Udam Samuel Aseer , an Internal Displaced Person ( IDP ) from the be ? sieged community , could not hide his grief . " A two-year-old child is buried on Children 's Day ... it is a symbol of every ? thing we have lost , " he lamented . " His future , our future , stolen by violence . " <p> Benue State , once proudly known as the " Food Basket of the Nation , " is now a land filled with fear and despair . For nearly a decade , swathes of the state have been relentlessly attacked , resulting in death , destruction , and displacement . Villages are deserted , communities are shattered , and the cries of orphaned children reverber ? ate through overcrowded IDP camps . <p> " With these attacks and killings , hunger and poverty have quickly set in , " says Dr. Thomas Terna Uzah , a Mass Communication expert and se ? nior lecturer at Hensard University Toru Orua in Bayelsa State . " A once-food basket of the nation can no lon ? ger farm , can not feed , and crops that have already been planted are being methodically destroyed by these devil reincarnates . The irony is agonising : a fertile region now struggling to feed its own people . " <p> The week of May 25th , 2025 , will be etched in the collective memory of Benue as a period of unimaginable horror . Over 42 people were brutally killed in the Gwer-West Local Govern ? ment Area alone , while seven others were critically injured and two were kidnapped . The communities of Aon ? dona , Ahume , Tyolaha , and Orbiam were in mourning , with residents fleeing in terror as the attackers de ? scended on them . <p> According to a local source who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation , the attacks were well-planned and brutal . " The armed Fu ? lani herders first attacked Aondona town on Sunday around 4 p.m. and continued yesterday at Ahume and a military base in Orbiam and Tyolaha . " The scale of the carnage is stagger ? ing : " I can categorically confirm to you that 20 people were killed in Aondona , five in Tyolaha , seven in Ahume , and six more were killed in Orbiam at the Military Base , which is only three ki ? lometres from Naka town , while sev ? en people were injured and two others kidnapped . " <p> The consequences are devastating . " As I speak with you , our people have fled every community in the affected areas . The entire community has been deserted and taken over by herders , " the source stated . " We can no longer go to farms , children can not attend school , and markets and churches have been closed as a result of these Fulani terrorists occupying commu ? nities . " <p> Hon. Victor Ormin , Chairman of the Gwer-West Local Government Council , confirmed the grim reality , calling the situation " pathetic . " He stated that the recovery of corpses was still ongoing , with over 30 bodies discovered in just two days . " I buried five people yesterday , fathers of chil ? dren , " he said , his voice full of emo ? tion . " Look at a two-year-old butchered with cutlasses . " <p> The Chairman 's frustration is palpable . He described a disturbing encounter with military personnel stationed nearby . " When I confronted the military about engaging the killers of my people , they stated that they are awaiting a directive from higher au ? thorities . " This alleged inaction has contributed to a growing sense of abandonment and betrayal among the affected communities . " So , my people must be killed before the federal gov ? ernment will talk about it ; what does this mean ? " Hon. Ormin enquired , his voice tinged with anger and despair . " This is genocidal . " <p> His frustration is understandable . " We are not claiming that the military is incompetent ; rather , the soldiers are awaiting orders and mandates to car ? ry out their duties , which have yet to be issued . " The lack of timely inter ? vention has left communities vulner ? able and exposed , feeding a cycle of violence and displacement . <p> Adding insult to injury , the Benue State Police Command has been con ? spicuously silent . Every attempt to ob ? tain confirmation or comment from the command 's police public relations officer , CSP Catherine Anene , was met with silence . The silence is deafening , eroding public trust and exacerbating feelings of abandonment . <p> A leaked security alert , purported ? ly from an intelligence source , detail ? ing the alleged plans of Fulani herders adds to the tragedy 's complexity . The alert , dated May 26th , 2025 , states that a meeting was held in the Agyaragu settlement in Nasarawa State , where plans were allegedly devised to attack several Benue communities . The alert even described a disturbing payment plan for militia members based on the number of Tiv people killed . Whether or not this intelligence was correct , the fact remains that attacks occurred in the designated areas , raising serious concerns about the responsiveness of security forces and the government . <p> The situation in Benue has not gone unnoticed , but the reaction from some quarters has been deeply dis ? turbing . Nuhu Ribadu , the National Security Adviser , recently paid a visit to Benue to address the crisis . Howev ? er , his comments have sparked outrage and disbelief . Instead of acknowledg ? ing the gravity of the situation , he played down the violence , claiming it was part of a global trend and denying that terrorists controlled any part of Nigeria . <p> " He told a bewildered nation that no part of Nigeria is in the hands of terrorists , " an undisclosed source stated . " He also stated that we are not doing badly in terms of security . " This is coming from someone who should have access to the most reliable securi ? ty intelligence in the country . " <p> The Middle Belt Forum ( MBF ) strongly condemns Ribadu 's remarks . In a press statement signed by Nation ? al Spokesman Luka Binniyat , the MBF expressed " deep concern " about the NSA 's comments . " What should have been a solemn , compassionate visit has turned into a contentious de ? velopment , " the statement said . <p> The MBF stated that many commu ? nities in Benue State , as well as parts of Southern Kaduna , Plateau , Niger , Kebbi , Sokoto , Katsina , and Zamfara states , are still under the control of armed militants . They also high ? lighted Borno Governor Babagana Zulum 's admission that Boko Haram has regained control of areas from which they were previously expelled . <p> " The MBF is thus alarmed and per ? plexed by the NSA 's statements , " the statement read . <p> " Who is briefing him ? On what grounds does he dismiss credible re ? ports of occupation and atrocities ? His remarks are not only inaccurate , but also callous , especially given that so many IDPs are living in subhuman conditions , stripped of their dignity , homes , and livelihoods . <p> The MBF expressed additional concerns about the ongoing " North Central Workshop on Developing a Na ? tional Framework on Disarmament , Demobilisation , and Reintegration " being held in Makurdi by the NSA 's office . They expressed concern that this framework would align with a contentious amnesty program in Ka ? duna State , which granted amnesty to " repentant " terrorists while ignoring the victims of their crimes . <p> The MBF strongly opposes any blanket amnesty for terrorists , claim ? ing that justice must be served . They also support the right to self-defence for besieged communities , as well as the establishment of state and local policing structures . <p> In response to the outcry , NSA Riba ? du reiterated the federal government 's commitment to addressing insecurity in Benue State . He referred to the re ? cent killings as a " national tragedy " and expressed support for the affected communities . <p> " What happened is a tragedy , an act of evil , " Ribadu stated during a stake ? holders ' meeting in Makurdi . " But when evil appears , good people must band together to confront it . We will work together to solve this problem . Do not feel alone ; this challenge affects everyone . " <p> He acknowledged the gravity of the crisis and expressed President Bola Tinubu 's solidarity with the people of Benue during this difficult time . Riba ? du also mentioned progress made in reducing the levels of violence that the current administration inherited , noting that efforts to improve security across the country are ongoing . <p> Despite the ongoing crisis , Benue State Governor Hyacinth Alia has re ? jected calls to declare a state of emer ? gency . He believes that the insecurity in Benue is not beyond his control and that he can manage the situation with more assistance from the federal gov ? ernment . <p> " What we need to do is get our people back home and drive out the invaders , the armed invaders who have brought in people who do not even speak the Nigerian languages . " <p> He emphasised that his govern ? ment has already made strides in reducing the number of local govern ? ments under attack , demonstrating its ability to control the violence . " We could not have reduced it from 17 local governments on the front lines of the attacks to nine , and now to six , indi ? cating that we can do so , but we need assistance . And that is a fact . <p> The situation in Benue State is dire , but not hopeless . There is a growing chorus of voices calling for immediate action to end the violence and bring justice to the victims . <p> Chief Sebastine Tar Hon , a Se ? nior Advocate of Nigeria ( SAN ) , has written to the Chief of Defence Staff , Gen. Christopher Gwabin Musa , the Inspector-General of Police , Egbe ? tokun , and the Director-General of the Department of State Services , Adeola Oluwatosin Ajayi , urging a strategic overhaul of operations to stem the tide of violence and save innocent lives . <p> Chief Hon emphasised the recent surge in deadly attacks , noting that more than 166 people were reported killed across various Local Govern ? ment Areas in the State in May alone . <p> He criticised recent military strate ? gies , citing insufficient deployment of police personnel and conflicting directives that may impede coordi ? nated efforts . <p> " Killings in the State by the invad ? ers have become a daily occurrence , and no one is challenging the murder ? ers , " Chief Hon stated . " Benue people are greeted daily with reports of their loved ones being killed , maimed , at ? tacked , and relocated from their an ? cestral lands . What a significant exis ? tential challenge for the good people of Benue State ! " <p> Senator Titus Zam , who represents Benue North East , has also been urged to take action in the Senate . In a letter to the Senator , Nick Agule urged him to summon the CDS and service chiefs to explain the lack of effective security despite the large budget allocation . He also advocated for legislation allowing citizens to carry firearms for self-de ? fence and addressing the deployment of security personnel to private indi ? viduals and government officials . <p> Amidst the despair and uncer ? tainty , the Tiv people have delivered a powerful message of resilience and determination . His Royal Majesty , the Tor Tiv , Prof. James Iorzua Or ? tese Ayatse has issued an ultimatum to herders occupying Tiv land : leave immediately . <p> The subjects , like many others , ex ? pressed full support for the Tor Tiv 's directive . " Our people have suffered in silence for far too long , " they said . " Our fathers ' farms have become bat ? tlegrounds , our mothers ' homes have become ruins , and our children 's fu ? ture is jeopardised by displacement and fear . " <p> The TorTiv people emphasised that their action is not a call to violence , but rather a call to peace and justice , or ? der , law , and the dignity of indigenous rights . " When you take a Tiv man 's land by force , you are attempting to eradicate a people . We will not let that happen . " <p> The unfolding tragedy in Benue State serves as a stark reminder of the human toll of conflict and the critical need for effective governance , justice , and peace . The cries of Benue children , buried on a day set aside for celebration , must not be ignored . It is critical to their survival and the future of their communities . <p> The recent approval of the National Forest Guard has sparked a national debate , highlighting the challenges of combating insecurity in Nigeria 's vast forest regions . The initiative , which involves deploying a specially trained and armed force across the country 's vulnerable forest zones , aims to reclaim these ungoverned territories from kidnappers , bandits , and insurgents . While supporters hail it as a bold step forward , critics raise serious concerns about militarisation , inter-agency conflicts , and the safety of the guards . ROLAND OGBONNAYA , TITILOPE JOSEPH , and SEYI TAIWO-OGUNTUASE examine the Forest Guard initiative from various perspectives , examining both its potential benefits and the critical challenges that must be addressed for it to succeed , as well as the anxieties about equipping untrained youth , revealing deep-seated concerns about Nigeria 's security landscape and the path forward . <p> National Forest Guards in Nigeria play a crucial role in protecting the country 's forests and combating deforestation . Their key functions include regular patrol of forest reserves to detect and deter illegal activities like logging , poaching , and encroachment as well as enforce forestry laws and regulations , arresting offenders and confiscating illegally obtained forest products.They also detect and suppress wildfires to protect forest resources , educate local communities on sustainable forest management practices and the importance of conservation , collect data on forest resources , biodiversity , and illegal activities to inform management decisions.In doing these , they work with other law enforcement agencies and organisations to combat environmental crimes . In essence , they are the front line in protecting Nigeria 's forests , conserving biodiversity , and ensuring sustainable use of forest resources . <p> President Bola Tinubu 's recent approval of the National Forest Guards ' new responsibilities of flushing out bandits , kidnappers , and insurgents from the forests sparked a national debate , with opinions ranging from enthusiastic support to deep scepticism . <p> The initiative , aimed at combating growing insecurity in Nigeria 's vast forest regions , seeks to deploy a specially trained and armed force throughout the country 's 1,129 designated forest zones , which are increasingly being exploited by kidnappers , bandits , and insurgent groups . While supporters see it as a bold step towards reclaiming ungoverned territories , critics are concerned about potential militarisation , inter-agency conflicts , and the safety of the proposed guards themselves . <p> The announcement , made by Special Adviser to the President on Media and Public Communication , Sunday Dare , emphasises the dire situation in these forested areas . " These areas have increasingly become safe havens for kidnappers , bandits , and insurgent groups , complicating government efforts to ensure rural community safety , " Dare explained . The operation is envisioned as a joint effort between the federal and state governments , with recruitment and training overseen by the Office of the National Security Adviser ( ONSA ) and the Federal Ministry of Environment . The plan is to arm the guards , allowing them to confront and dismantle criminal networks , while also addressing youth unemployment by bringing thousands of young Nigerians into the force . <p> President Tinubu has reaffirmed his commitment to national sovereignty , stating that " every inch of Nigeria must remain under the control of legitimate authorities . " <p> While the initiative is gaining support from some , many Nigerians have expressed deep concerns . However , the initiative has been met with widespread concern , particularly about the safety and training of the proposed forest guards . An anonymous source , possibly reflecting public concerns , expressed his thoughts on social media , describing the initiative as a " officially " sanctioned " voluntary suicide mission . " He claimed that using " untrained youth " against " well-armed criminals " is equivalent to " official ' premeditated ' murder . " He also expressed concern that arming a large number of young people would lead to the formation of militias with ethnic and religious implications . The source concludes that establishing State Police is preferable to a " fire brigade approach . " <p> Miss Olivia Aniunoh , Senior Legal , Policy , and Research Analyst at Nextier , acknowledges that the initiative addresses a critical gap in Nigeria 's internal security architecture but emphasises the importance of execution . She believes that the decision to establish a National Forest Guard fills " a critical gap in Nigeria 's internal security architecture , namely the governance vacuum in forested areas . " However , she warns that " without a comprehensive framework for training , oversight , and integration with existing institutions ... the forest guard initiative risks becoming yet another poorly coordinated paramilitary entity . " <p> She also expresses concern about the NSA 's oversight , implying a possible conflict between security priorities and environmental stewardship . In her opinion , the government may be heading in the right direction , " but on shaky ground . " <p> Aniunoh also emphasises the possibility of positive change , stating that " strategically deployed forest guards could alter the security calculus in rural Nigeria by denying criminal groups safe havens . " However , she emphasises that this depends on " recruitment standards , quality of training , clarity of mandates , and , most importantly , community trust and cooperation . " Furthermore , she expresses concern about the already " bloated and poorly coordinated " security architecture , emphasising the need for " structural reforms " and " clear lines of command " to prevent further institutional confusion . <p> Several commentators have echoed Aniunoh 's concerns about Nigeria 's already crowded security landscape , citing the proliferation of security agencies . According to Goddy Uwazurike , a lawyer and President of Credibility Group , the country currently has " the police , immigration , customs , prisons , road safety , NSDC , Coast Guards , EFCC , DSS , army , navy , and air force , " all with overlapping mandates . <p> Aniunoh also expresses concern about Nigerian society 's increasing militarisation and the potential erosion of human rights . She concludes that " security must be people-centered , not weapon-centered , " calling for investment in " intelligence , justice , livelihoods , and civic trust . " <p> Femi Aborishade , a human rights lawyer , is also skeptical , claiming that the initiative " does not address the fundamental root cause of physical insecurity , namely unprecedented poverty . " He believes that the government 's emphasis on a " military ( kinetic ) solution rather than addressing policies that have exacerbated poverty ( the non-kinetic solution ) is misguided . " <p> According to Aborishade , if the Forest Guards are not properly trained and equipped , they may become " sacrificial lamb(s) in the hands of Boko Haram insurgents with sophisticated weapons . " He advocates for addressing the root causes of insecurity through anti-poverty measures and empowering citizens to defend themselves , as well as strengthening existing regional security forces . <p> Goddy Uwazurike emphasises the disparity between forest guards ' intended role and the nature of the threats they will encounter . He claims that a " forest guard mentally is a civilian and not a person poised to shoot and kill like a soldier , " and states that " the average terrorist is prepared to kill on sight . " He proposes the formation of a specialised " Forest Corp , " similar to a marine or armoured corps , capable of defeating terrorists . <p> Adewale Adeoye , Executive Director of Journalists for Democratic Rights ( JODER ) , emphasises the need for rigorous training , modern equipment , and community involvement to ensure the initiative 's success . He warns against political interference in the recruitment process , emphasising the importance of selecting educated , passionate , and dedicated individuals based on merit . Adeoye envisions forest guards using drones , establishing bush camps , and prioritising human rights education . <p> Yerima Shettima , President General of the Arewa Youths Consultative Forum ( AYCF ) , believes that the National Forest Guard has the potential to improve intelligence gathering and community engagement . He stated that a localised approach could allow for faster responses to threats and foster trust between law enforcement and communities , which is critical for effective policing . <p> According to Comrade Aghedo Kehinde , Convener of Vanguard Liberations , deploying trained personnel equipped for bush surveillance and rural patrol addresses the root of the problem by denying criminals their strongest advantage : safe havens . <p> Despite the criticism , some security analysts and community leaders believe the National Forest Guard has great potential . Comrade Ajayi Popoola , an activist , points out that the country 's forests have become a haven for criminal activity in recent years . <p> Hon. Ebube Ebisike George , SOAD Minister of Trade , contends that if properly deployed with sincerity and not a propaganda-driven or quota-based system in which merit guides the recruitment process , the National Forest Guards program can be successful and significantly alter the dynamics of the insecurity challenge . George also believes that if the Forests were properly managed and organised into taskforces with competent and uninducible leaders overseeing the process , the insecurity crisis would have been avoided long ago . <p> Victor Okpara , SAN , acknowledges that the criminality that exists will overwhelm the guards . He still believes they are important to have as forest guards . " You know , we are in an era of global warming , " he said , " so it is a good move on the part of the government to ensure that the focus is on afforestation rather than deforestation . " To that end , it is an admirable step . Will it protect us ? " Probably , but not entirely . " <p> Okechukwu Nwanguma , Executive Director of RULAAC , emphasises the importance of transparency and community participation in the establishment of Forest Guards as a response to Nigeria 's escalating security challenges . He argued that " the establishment of local policing initiatives such as Forest Guards is a necessary response to the Nigeria Police 's inadequacies in protecting lives and property . " He emphasises that " Forest Guards must be drawn from within the communities they are expected to protect , " emphasising the value of community trust and understanding of local dynamics . He also emphasises the importance of adequate funding , training , and supervision , as well as clearly defined accountability frameworks . <p> Ige Asemudara , a Lagos-based lawyer , believes the project is welcome . Asemudara stated that " insecurity is a major concern , and we can only discuss merging or reducing the number of security agencies once we have achieved a sufficient level of safety . " Until then , any legitimate effort to improve security should be encouraged . " He also emphasises the importance of strategic deployment in areas they are familiar with . <p> The debate over the National Forest Guard highlights Nigeria 's complex challenges in combating insecurity . While the initiative is a bold attempt to reclaim ungoverned spaces , its success is dependent on addressing several critical issues , such as comprehensive training and equipment . Forest guards must undergo rigorous training to equip them with the skills required to confront well-armed criminals while upholding human rights . They must also be given modern equipment and technology to effectively monitor and patrol large forested areas.Others are community engagement and trust , as the initiative must prioritise community participation and foster trust between forest guards and local residents . Recruitment should prioritise individuals with strong ties to the communities they serve , ensuring sensitivity to local dynamics and instilling a sense of shared responsibility for security.Inter-agency coordination and streamlining are critical because the government must address the existing fragmentation within the security architecture by establishing clear lines of command , harmonising operational doctrines , and integrating intelligence systems . Streamlining existing agencies and clarifying roles is critical to avoiding turf wars and duplication of effort.In addition , the underlying causes of insecurity must be addressed . The government must address the underlying socioeconomic factors that contribute to insecurity , such as poverty , unemployment , and a lack of opportunity . Investing in development programs that generate jobs and foster civic trust is critical for long-term stability.Transparency and accountability are also important because the initiative must be implemented in a transparent and accountable manner , ensuring that forest guards are held accountable for their actions and that abuses of power are investigated and addressed immediately . Independent oversight mechanisms are required to keep the force from becoming a source of human rights violations . <p> The National Forest Guard represents both an opportunity and a risk . If implemented carefully and strategically , it could help to reclaim ungoverned territories , improve community safety , and address youth unemployment . However , without careful planning , adequate resources , and a commitment to good governance , it risks becoming yet another poorly coordinated , ineffective , and potentially dangerous addition to Nigeria 's already complex security environment . Ultimately , the success of the initiative will depend on the government 's ability to balance security concerns with the broader needs of governance , community development , and respect for human rights . <p> Nigeria , a country rich in mineral resources , is facing a monumental crisis : billions of dollars in losses due to rampant illegal mining . While efforts to combat this illegal activity have increased , the fight is proving extremely difficult , especially since the " enemies within " -- corrupt officials and powerful vested interests -- are actively undermining these efforts , perpetuating the cycle of economic loss and environmental devastation . ROLAND OGBONNAYA writes <p> Nigeria , a country endowed with abundant natural resources , continues to grapple with the pernicious issue of illegal mining . While the oil and gas sector has long dominated the country 's economy , the solid minerals sector has enormous opportunities for diversification and economic growth . However , this poten ? tial is severely hampered by widespread illegal mining activities , which cost the country trillions of naira each year and contribute to insecurity , environmental degradation , and social unrest . <p> In 2023 , Nigeria 's solid minerals sector contributed 0.77% of the country 's GDP , a slight decrease from 0.84% in 2022 . While this figure appears insignificant , it hides the sector 's true potential . " This modest contribution represents the sector 's po ? tential to grow and contribute more to the economy if illegal mining and other atrocities are stopped , " according to a recent report . The issue is not a scarcity of resources , but a failure to effectively manage and regulate them . <p> Illegal mining in Nigeria takes many forms , ranging from artisanal miners working without a licence to sophisti ? cated networks involving powerful in ? dividuals and foreign entities . In their research paper " Curtailing Illegal Mining Operation in Nigeria , " Amosu C.O. and Adeosun T.A . define it as " mining activity undertaken without permission of the state or government , particularly in the absence of land rights , mining licenses , and exploration or mineral rights . " They also stated that since independence in 1960 , illegal mining has continued un ? abated , and no royalties have been paid to the federal government due to the lack of an effective policy . <p> These operations thrive on a number of factors , including poor governance , in ? sufficient monitoring , corruption , and a lack of economic opportunities for local communities . Professor Akinade Olatun ? ji , president of the Nigerian Mining and Geosciences Society ( NMGS ) , emphasis ? es the importance of proper funding for federal mining offices in each state . " Each state has a federal mines office , and each office should be adequately staffed and equipped , " he argues . <p> He emphasises that illegal mining activities are primarily concentrated in rural communities , necessitating that state offices be well-equipped with ve ? hicles and adequate operating costs to enable effective monitoring . " The feder ? al government must stop lip service and ensure that mining offices are properly equipped . We oppose illegal mining be ? cause it harms the environment . " <p> The effects of illegal mining are far-reaching and devastating . Economic Losses : Illegal mining causes Nigeria to lose trillions of naira each year . Accord ? ing to Jonathan Gbefwi , chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on Solid Minerals , illegal mining costs the country approximately $9 billion per year . This represents a significant loss of potential revenue that could have gone towards infrastructure development , education , and healthcare . <p> Environmental Degradation : Illegal mining practices frequently involve the use of hazardous chemicals and unsus ? tainable methods , resulting in extensive environmental degradation . Deforesta ? tion , soil erosion , water pollution , and ecosystem destruction are all possible consequences of mineral extraction . Amosu and Adeosun point out that ille ? gal miners use crude methods that can re ? sult in mine collapses , leaving " craters on the land " that become dangerous " mining ponds " when it rains , contaminated with acidic and poisonous metallic residue . <p> Toxic substances used in illegal min ? ing pose significant health risks to local communities . The infamous lead poison ? ing incident in Zamfara State serves as a sobering reminder of the disastrous consequences . Amosu and Adeosun cited media reports at the time indicating that lead concentrations in the atmosphere of some homes had reached 23,000 parts per million , which was significantly higher than the 400 parts per million thresh ? old considered safe by the Ministry of Mines and Steel Development . " Katsina and Zamfara States are evidence of acute lead poisoning caused by ore processing , contaminating the local river where they fetch drinking water , affecting over 3,500 children and killing over 400 adults . " <p> Fuelling Insecurity : Illegal mining has become inextricably linked to inse ? curity in some parts of Nigeria , partic ? ularly the North West . The proceeds of illegal mining are frequently used to fund criminal activities such as banditry , kid ? napping , and armed conflict . " There is also an inseparable link between illegal mining operations and the festering in ? security in the North-West region , where the criminal enterprise thrives . " <p> Nigeria 's solid minerals sector , brim ? ming with potential and housing at least one commercial mineral in every state , is hemorrhaging billions of dollars annual ? ly due to rampant illegal mining and ex ? port practices . From gold to lithium , the country 's resources are dwindling , aided by a complex web of factors ranging from unregulated artisanal mining to alleged collusion by powerful " enemies within . " <p> During a candid interview with Sat ? urday INDEPENDENT this week , Hon. Ebube Ebisike George , SOAD Minister of Trade , highlighted the staggering scope of the problem . " Nigeria is estimated to lose approximately $9 billion in gold per year due to illegal export practices , " he stated . This figure represents gold smuggled out of the country without going through official channels , poten ? tially evading taxes and depriving the country of vital revenue . He claimed the problem extends beyond gold . Accord ? ing to the Nigeria Extractive Industry Transparency Initiative ( NEITI ) , artis ? anal miners account for 80% of Nigeria 's mining activity , and their operations are largely unregulated . The NEITI estimates that losses from illegal mining of other minerals total $2-3 billion per year , with some estimates suggesting even higher amounts . Dr. Dieter Bassi , NEITI 's techni ? cal director , echoed this sentiment during a speaking engagement , revealing that , according to ECOWAS , illegal activity costs Nigeria a staggering 91% of its mining revenue each year . <p> " The Bola Tinubu-led government has acknowledged the gravity of the situation and has taken steps to address it . Minister Oladele Alake has established a specially trained Mining Marshal force of 2,220 Ni ? gerian Security and Civil Defence Corps ( NSCDC ) personnel , with 60 assigned to each state to protect the mining environ ? ment and combat illegal miners . " <p> Hon. Ebisike George , on the other hand , emphasised the complexities of the issue , stating , " The NSCDC is doing their best , but they only serve as an initial barrier to illegal mining activities . Other security forces , such as the Army , Air Force , DSS , and others , are also contributing to the larger effort to improve the security archi ? tecture required to combat illegal mining through arrest and kinetic means . " <p> The most damning accusation is the alleged involvement of powerful figures . " The most significant challenge confront ? ing government agencies and the NSCDC is that the political elite , security force leadership , and their cronies with private jets are internal collaborators who allow foreigners to articulate massive theft of Nigeria 's solid minerals . " These are the core ' enemies within ' the economic sys ? tem , " Hon. Ebisike George declared . <p> He used ongoing allegations between Zamfara 's current governor and his pre ? decessor , who is now Minister of State for Defence , as an example . <p> Senator Adams Oshiomohle , Edo State 's former governor , echoed these con ? cerns in public . However , Hon. Ebisike George is calling for a " strategic action plan by the APC Tinubu Government that does not protect any sacred cows and should include a comprehensive purge of those in government fingered in banditry sponsorship and linked to illegal mining of gold and other minerals . " <p> Looking ahead , Hon. Ebisike George stressed the importance of empowering indigenous mining companies . He advo ? cates for strong government assistance in the form of favourable policies and increased investment , particularly from institutions like the Bank of Industry . This includes funding for cutting-edge technology , employee training , and safety improvements . <p> " A thriving and healthy mining in ? dustry is a huge tax earner for the gov ? ernment and people , " he asserts , " which translates into larger corporate social responsibility ( CSR ) footprints for the communities that host these companies . " <p> Furthermore , he advocates for in ? creased monitoring of mining sites via satellite technology and drones , as well as strict pollution controls , to mitigate the negative effects on water resources , farmland , and the environment . <p> According to Hon. Ebisike George , " the entire solid minerals sector requires sanitisation based on political will , im ? pact investment , strategic technology collaborations , and monitoring . " Only through a concerted effort , targeting both visible illegal miners and " enemies within , " will Nigeria be able to realise the full potential of its mineral wealth and ensure a prosperous future for its people . <p> The Nigerian government recognis ? es the gravity of the illegal mining crisis and has taken some steps to address it . At that time , much of the continent 's risk capital was flowing outwards , with little capacity to retain premiums or build local underwriting expertise . <p> What @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pan-African powerhouse , operating in over 50 African countries with regional offices in strategic economic hubs such as Nairobi , Abidjan , Tunis , Douala , Gaborone and Lagos . <p> Over the years , the reinsurer 's role has evolved to a key architect of Africa 's risk architecture . <p> By providing both life and non-life reinsurance solutions , ranging from fire , engineering , marine and aviation to agriculture , Continental Re has filled a critical void in the continent 's insurance value chain . " It further reveals that 56% of over 2,000 public health issues examined between 2001 and 2021 in Africa are climate change-induced . <p> For clarity , climate change is driven by rising temperature which manifests as global warming . Global warming is caused by greenhouse gases emitted to the atmosphere . In his book , How to Avoid Climate Disaster , Bill Gates records that fifty-one ( 51 ) billion tons of greenhouse gases were cumulatively added to the global atmosphere before the 2020 COVID-19 lock-down . Emitted greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere and in turn @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with more emissions , the global temperature rises higher . And since the year 1850 , emissions of greenhouse gases have remained on a dramatic increase . <p> Carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) is a major greenhouse gas with about 74% of the global overall . Despite the stronger potency of emitted gases from methane ( CH4 ) and nitrous oxide ( N20 ) , CO2 's higher concentration and long stay in the atmosphere makes it the core driver of human-induced climate change . Thus , about " one-fifth of the carbon dioxide emitted today will still be there in 10,000 years . " CO2 is generated from human activities such as burning of fossil fuels , industrial byproducts , deforestation , and certain agricultural practices ( enteric fermentation during livestock digestion and anthropogenic methane in flooded rice paddies ) . <p> Water vapour is also a greenhouse gas , but it stays for a while in the air and falls back as rain or snow to the earth 's surface . The natural sources of greenhouse gases like volcanic eruptions , respiration , decomposition , and emissions from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as human-induced greenhouse gas . The first is the expansion of waters . When oceans warm up , they increase in volume . The second is the melting of land ice , that is , mountain glaciers . The big ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica contribute significantly to the rising of sea level . However , the revelation that in the last 2,000 years , sea level was stable but by the late 19th century , it began to rise continually , is worrisome . However , despite its importance , dredging in Nigeria faces several challenges that are deeply rooted in geographical , regulatory , and economic complexities . <h> A Growing Need for Dredging <p> Nigeria 's rivers and coastline have long served as important transportation and economic corridors . However , with increased siltation , encroaching sandbars @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ navigable . As a result , dredging is frequently required for river dredging operations , port access , and flood management . Additionally , the continuous need for coastal erosion control is pushing both public and private stakeholders to invest in long-term dredging strategies . <p> Unfortunately , the regional challenges across Africa make consistent progress difficult . <h> Environmental and Regulatory Hurdles <p> One of the primary issues facing dredging in Nigeria is regulatory inconsistency . Multiple layers of local , state , and federal governance often result in conflicting permits , unclear environmental impact standards , and delayed approvals . These delays are especially critical when dealing with waterway infrastructure development , which requires timely intervention to prevent disruptions in transportation and trade . <p> Furthermore , environmental concerns -- such as disturbance to aquatic ecosystems , resettlement of nearby communities , and improper disposal of dredged materials -- must be addressed with sensitive planning and oversight . Without clear environmental frameworks , these concerns can result in halted projects or long-term ecological damage . <h> Infrastructure and Equipment Gaps <p> Dredging projects in Africa , particularly in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ equipment and trained personnel . Many small operators rely on outdated or makeshift dredging machines that are inefficient and prone to breakdowns . This gap is particularly evident in more remote or underfunded regions where access to quality dredging tools and support is limited . <p> Dredge Flow continues to advocate for partnerships that bring in more sustainable equipment and technical expertise into local markets . The goal is not only to improve project efficiency but also to increase safety and long-term results . <h> Socio-Economic Factors <p> The intersection of dredging with socio-economic development can not be overlooked . On the one hand , dredging stimulates job creation and enables trade by maintaining waterways . On the other hand , unregulated dredging practices can lead to land disputes , environmental degradation , and the displacement of communities . Balancing these outcomes is one of the more delicate challenges in regions already affected by limited infrastructure and governance gaps . <p> Moreover , due to Nigeria 's urban expansion and land reclamation initiatives , the demand for dredged sand has skyrocketed . This creates incentives for illegal dredging , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ legitimate infrastructure development . <h> Regional Differences in Africa <p> While dredging in Nigeria faces its localized challenges , other African nations also struggle with similar yet context-specific issues . In East Africa , for example , fluctuating lake levels and sedimentation affect inland port operations . In West Africa , rising sea levels have accelerated the need for coastal erosion control , particularly in countries like Ghana and Sierra Leone . <p> These shared challenges highlight the need for collaborative efforts , shared technologies , and investment in capacity building across the continent . <h> The Way Forward <p> Despite these obstacles , opportunities for improvement remain . Creating unified regulatory frameworks and enforcing strict environmental standards will help ensure that waterway infrastructure development is sustainable and community-friendly . <p> Additionally , incorporating local expertise and involving affected communities in decision-making processes can lead to better project outcomes and reduced conflict . @@127425096 <h> What Buhari meant to me <p> When I was seven , my young impressionable mind was awakened and awed by a certain general who emerged from the blue and strode like a colossus over the political atmosphere of Nigeria . The advent of his regime signalled a new era in the governance of the country , as the air became charged and the land became hot . Due to this officer and his men 's draconian principles , people suddenly adorned the awareness garb of their patriotic duties as citizens . They became more responsible , more disciplined , and more accountable ; albeit being forced to do so . <p> But more importantly , every citizen began to care for their immediate natural and artificial environment . I was born in a neighbourhood that could be best described as a ghetto in the context of modern urbanisation . Squalor was the reality of my childhood because it was entwined with the everyday life of the urban poor . Even when my parents were apostles of cleanliness and order , one could not help but choke under the neighbourly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ filth of the ' amenities-challenged ' community . <p> So , it was like salvation when Major-General Muhammadu Buhari struck on New Year 's Eve , 1983 . I remember it like yesterday . My family and I were enjoying our Christmas holiday in the village , which was an annual ritual for most families from my side of the country . One early morning , just when the parents and their children were about to begin preparations to journey back to the city to resume their hustle and their schooling , respectively , my father 's transistor radio began to blare some strange-sounding monotonous music . Being a movie buff at a young age , I knew it sounded like war-tunes . <p> Then I noticed the worry on my parents ' faces . There were whispers in anxious tones . I was a very imaginative child and could not help but begin to visualise the stories they had earlier told us about the Biafran War . My mother , who was a teenager during the war , could paint startlingly vivid pictures of how she , her siblings @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to another other avoiding the Nigerian military advance into the South-Eastern heartland . I could not help but wonder whether another war was in the offing . <p> Thankfully , within hours , the coast was clear . The adults said it was a coup d ' ? tat . That was all I was told ; nobody explained anything to me . Yet , the worried mien never left their faces . It was when we arrived in Enugu that everything became clear to me . The atmosphere in the city was tense and uncertain . You could feel dread in the air . They said politicians were being arrested . They said they were corrupt . They said they hid roomfuls of cash . They said Buhari would rid the country of bad people . Every bad thing would be swept out of Nigeria . <p> Lo and behold , people began to sweep . I saw adults sweep , and children mop . We started to exorcise the spirit of squalor from our district , then popularly known as ' Oba Jongle ' ( Urban Jungle ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at what we could accomplish . People were afraid to drop food wrappings on the ground . Families procured dust bins and waste disposal drums . There were all sizes of them . Some were fabricated in shapeless forms and painted with funny colours . I would walk around the neighbourhood admiring the different designs and colours from families that did not have the resources to buy ready-made waste bins . My father bought a grey aluminium type and painted our family name on it . <p> Indeed , I began to fall in love with Buhari . I also began to toy with the idea of joining the military to be like him when I grew up . I knew I loathed violence , but anything was good for me as long as we were cleaning up the country 's dirty environment and chasing away the bad people . <p> Then came the icing on the cake . Suddenly , army trucks packed full of fierce-looking , koboko-wielding soldiers , careened into Oba Jongle and began to enforce what was to become a new economic order . I ran @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ food items and distribute them to ghetto dwellers . I heard that the merchants were guilty of some crimes . This time , they were sharing nutritious food items to families . My mother also queued up to get some : rice , beverages , detergents , sugar , name them . It was a bazaar . <p> However , it was not only about the good time . My father suddenly did not have ' cash ' like he used to . His apprentices whispered to me that they were queuing up in banks for hours on end to get their old naira notes exchanged for new ones . But they were only able to get less than half exchanged . After some time , the gritty voice of one soldier who introduced himself as ' Dogonyaro ' , told us that Buhari was out , with his revolutionary war-against-indiscipline and environmental-sanitation . The rest is history . <p> But for me , my life was already on a trajectory that would never reverse or change course . Right from that day , I subconsciously followed issues that pertained to the environment . Pursuant to this dream , I published a small book in 2006 , entitled " The Plan for Nigeria " , where I analysed Buhari 's green credentials , and praised him to the high heavens . In fact , when Buhari eventually won the election in 2015 , some people called me from across the country to congratulate me on a " prophecy come true " . <p> Yet , I must confess that I felt disappointed that President Buhari did not stick to the six principles of the Global Greens Charter : Ecological wisdom , social justice , participatory democracy , nonviolence , sustainability , and respect for diversity . Developed regions like Europe and North America now see net reforestation , while Africa continues to lose about 3.9 M ha annually . Key success stories include the United States , where heavy past deforestation reversed in the mid-20 th century . <p> Forest cover has been steadily increasing at 0.03% per year between 2010 and 2020 . European nations have similarly expanded forests through reforestation , strong regulation , and afforestation incentives @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Since 1900 , tropical regions have lost roughly 22% of their forested land , comparable to Amazon rates . C ? te d'Ivoire and Ghana lost approximately 80% of forests between 1900 and 2021 from agricultural expansion , while Kenya dropped from 10% to 1.7% forest cover between 1963 and 2006 . Madagascar lost over 90% of its original forest , and Ethiopia has only 2% remaining . <p> Weak accountability at both federal and state levels introduces risks of fund misappropriation . Also , security challenges including illegal logging backed by corruption , or forest encroachment supported by collusion in agency bureaucracies threaten enforcement unless security agencies like the Nigerian Forest Security Service are empowered and safeguarded . <p> Climate finance pipelines often come with stringent donor conditions , making bureaucracy and transparency essential or funding will be withheld . And markets such as the EU 's anti-deforestation due diligence regulation will require robust supply-chain traceability , absent which Nigerian producers could be excluded . <p> By inference , Nigeria must build the institutional capacity to comply , or risk losing access to key markets . Brazil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cattle , plus REDD+ payments . Payment for Ecosystem Services schemes , where communities are paid to maintain forests , are used in Costa Rica and parts of Europe but Nigeria 's REDD+ national strategy launched in 2023 currently lacks funding and local engagement . <p> While Nigeria 's federal government announced a chase of $2 billion forest economy fund , state-level implementation often falters due to overlapping jurisdictions as Nigeria is divided into 36 states and each with its own policies and complicating unified action . Corruption and lack of law enforcement exacerbate illegal logging . The federal government 's top-down rhetoric has yet to translate into proper funding , accountability , or rural community engagement . <p> One key step to combating deforestation and promoting sustainable forest management to protect livelihood in agriculture and prevent nutrient wash-way from top soil is scaling up Payment for Ecosystem Services ( PES ) and REDD+ initiatives , linking them to global carbon markets by channelling international funds such as the Green Climate Fund through transparent , village-level forest stewardship systems . <p> Advertisement <p> Empowering community forestry is also essential with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ communities . Harmonising federal and state policies will ensure consistency in forest definitions , land-use permits , and enforcement penalties across the country . Investments in satellite-based monitoring technologies can enhance real-time surveillance of deforestation , enabling more effective resource allocation and enforcement . <p> Sustainable agroforestry should be promoted through the provision of subsidised seeds , training programmes , and access to credit for tree-crop intercropping . Nigeria must also build its capacity to comply with export standards such as the EU 's Deforestation Regulation by mapping supply chains and issuing deforestation-free certifications . <p> Advertisement <p> A moratorium on the conversion of forests for high-risk commodities could serve as a necessary short-term measure to protect vital ecosystems . The country should prioritise climate-smart economic diversification , boosting sectors like ecotourism , sustainable timber , and the production of non-timber forest products such as medicinal plants and honey <p> To operationalise this vision , Nigeria must rigorously reform both institutional structures and policy instruments . First , the national Council on Climate Change which oversees Climate Act implementation must enable sub-national nodes in each state with clear roles in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Second , forest governance must shift from revenue-first to collaboration-first . <p> State governments should establish independent forestry commissions with fiscal autonomy and management oversight , enabling them to hold logging permits accountable , reinvest fees into regeneration programs , involve communities and civil society , and deploy modern tools like drones and geospatial mapping to track change . <p> Third , establishing community-based natural resource management ( CBNRM ) structures with incentives such as service-based payments , extension support , and clean energy alternatives can create stewardship and transform forest users into partners rather than adversaries . But to work , such models must include livelihood diversification in sustainable agroforestry systems , regulated fuel-wood harvesting , and training for local communities in governance and regeneration practices . Fourth , Nigeria must harness existing climate finance frameworks and climate diplomacy . <p> The Kunming -- Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework calls for at least USD 20 billion in biodiversity finance by 2025 for Global South countries which Nigeria can access a share of that by demonstrating credible commitments like its National Climate Change Fund , effective carbon budgeting , improved monitoring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ finance flows into Nigeria remain modest relative to ambition and risk diversion or mismanagement if institutional transparency is not strengthened . Nigeria should leverage ecosystems like mangroves and park reserves to pilot Natural Capital Accounting approaches that value forests not just for timber but for carbon , biodiversity , and tourism potential . <p> Focusing on ecosystem valuation , agrarian transformation through agroforestry , and forest economy options such as mangroves and ecotourism , Nigeria can build a forest-based development model . If implemented with transparency and accountability this integrated approach could transform Nigeria from a source of deforestation emissions into a leader in forest restoration , carbon sequestration , and climate-resilient rural prosperity . Without systemic reform , however , even bold plans like the proposed $2 billion forest economy fund risk becoming costly but ineffectual gestures . <p> Seyi Adedokun is a Nigerian freelance writer and research enthusiast . @@127455218 <p> In this file photo from February 2019 , judges are seen at the International Court of Justice File : Eva Plevier/Reuters <p> On July 23 , 2025 , the International Court of Justice ( ICJ ) issued a historic advisory opinion affirming that countries have binding obligations under international law to address climate change . Environmental destruction that harms people 's lives , livelihoods , and rights , the Court proclaimed , could amount to a violation of international law -- especially where vulnerable communities are affected . <p> This unprecedented ruling is a wake-up call for Nigeria . <p> From the devastating floods that inundate Bayelsa and other coastal states along the Niger and Benue rivers , to the steady advance of desertification in the Northwest and Northeast , Nigeria is already in the grip of a climate crisis . This crisis is perhaps most starkly reflected in the ongoing and often deadly southward movement of herders , commonly described as farmer-herder clashes , which has left a trail of violence and trauma across numerous communities . <p> For years , desertification and changing rainfall patterns have pushed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ In the absence of strong adaptation policies , this has led to violent clashes with farming communities , destroying lives and displacing millions . Entire villages in Benue , Plateau , and Taraba have been wiped out -- not just by bullets , but by a failure to protect the environment . <p> The ICJ ruling is a game-changer and situates the issue as a legal one . Governments are duty-bound to act when environmental mismanagement leads to conflict , suffering , and death . Citizens have a right to be protected from the risks of environmental mismanagement . What are the applicable provisions of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria ( as amended ) ? Sections 33 and 34 guarantee the right to life and dignity . Section 20 mandates the state to " protect and improve the environment and safeguard the water , air , land , forest and wildlife of Nigeria . " <p> The question Nigerians must now ask is : Has our government , as the duty bearer , fulfilled this duty ? <p> If herders are forced to migrate , it creates conflict with sedentary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ farmers are losing harvests due to heat and flooding . If families are displaced and made destitute because the climate is breaking down . Then we are facing a governance failure that may be unconstitutional and actionable . <p> The ICJ opinion marks a significant milestone for climate litigation globally . It provides a powerful legal basis that our lawyers , judges , and activists can now invoke to hold the government accountable -not only for its actions , but also for its inaction . This ruling reinforces the imperative that policies must align with principles , creating a critical opportunity to move beyond rhetoric and toward real , measurable progress on this vital issue . <p> It also strengthens Nigeria 's hand in international climate finance negotiations . With low historical emissions and high vulnerability , Nigeria should now press more forcefully for loss and damage funding , climate justice , and technology transfers , not as charity , but as a matter of global legal responsibility . <h> Related News <p> What must be done ? A coordinated , timely , and mutually reinforcing strategy is needed across @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the Constitution . Environmental protection is not a luxury but a legal duty . Let 's stop treating it like a footnote . <p> Second , integrate climate into security and agricultural planning . Solving the farmer-herder crisis requires water infrastructure , supporting the development of a modern approach to animal husbandry ( ranching ) , and early-warning systems , not just troops or curfews . <p> Third , support climate-related court cases . Nigerian courts must begin to treat environmental harm as a rights issue , not just a regulatory one . <p> Fourth , invest in resilience . From Lagos to Maiduguri , we must design cities and farms for a hotter , wetter , and more unpredictable future . <p> The ICJ 's advisory opinion reminds us that climate justice is not just a global concern . @@127455909 <h> Disinformation as Threat to Civil Service Function in Post-Truth World <h> Disinformation as Threat to Civil Service Function in Post-Truth World <p> Sunday , July 27 , 2025 3:58 pm <p> Professor Tunji Olaopaolaopa <p> By Tunji Olaopa <p> Lately , and in keeping faith with my research commitments , I had posed for myself the research question : what is that one most significant threat to the government bureaucracy , whether you call it the civil service , public service or the public administration system ; a threat to it as the veritable back-end engine room that governments rely on to deliver on their promises to the people and to fulfill development vision and programmes commitments in a democracy ? That one threat that keeps recurring , based on my investigation , is significantly disinformation or misinformation a la fake news ; the whole post-truth alacrity and the diminution of objective facts in favour sentimentalism and emotion , and its backdrop of expanding global populism in politics . Consequently and lately , I had been looking at such subjects as artificial intelligence , big data and data science @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , freedom of information policy , privacy in the dynamics of internet and social media governance , the Gen Z prospects as the workforce in the public service emerging future frontiers , and I can go on and on . <p> Indeed , it has become self-evident , according to Joseph Schumpeter , that the bureaucracy constitutes an inevitable complement to the success of democratic governance anywhere in the world . What is not evident is that there is a lot of conditions that intervene and interfere in the modern world in undermining the significant relationship that ought to hold between democratic governance and the bureaucracy . In other words , it is not automatic that the bureaucratic machineries and mechanisms of government will backstop the evolution of good governance . Indeed , many high-performing nations have witnessed significant transformation despite a not too remarkable , regarded , competent and a therefore heavily politicized civil service . Be that as it may , one key challenge that public administration system and the bureaucracy has always faced since its emergence in time is the increasing complexities of the human society arising @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . For instance , the increasing trajectory of human population provided a complicated phenomenon that tasked the capacity of the bureaucracy to manage the dynamics of policy design and implementation that cater for the welfare of the citizens in government development planning and the national transformation process . <p> In contemporary times , the challenges have become even more complex and perplexing such that bureaucracies across the world are struggling to make sense of the events that are now shaping the world . Scholars of geopolitics and international affairs are now designating the world as a VUCA -- vulnerable , uncertain , complex and ambiguous -- environment that is assailed by polycrisis . A polycrisis refers to the capacity of a crisis to morph into a complex form that draws on various other contingent but problematic issues . Climate change is a good example of how a crisis could become aggravated into a polycrisis . As a crisis on its own , the climate change issue references how human activities , especially the burning of fossil fuels , have undermined the ecological integrity of the earth . However , environmental @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to interconnect with and aggravate other critical issues to produce biodiversity loss , governance and infrastructural deficits , early warning failures , agricultural loss , pandemics , and finally civil unrests . This is the way a polycrisis manifests . <p> And public bureaucracies are supposed to serve as the middle point of intervention between citizens and polycrisis like climate change , especially in terms of policy designs that are sufficiently forward-looking in ways that alleviate how these crises affect their lives . In other words , the public bureaucracies are supposed to serve as the government 's instrument for making democratic governance a reality despite the scourges of complex polycrisis . Unfortunately , even the democratic experiment has generated its own fundamental challenge that complicates the capacity of the bureaucracy to complement a democratic state and its capacity to deliver democratic governance . What I mean to say is that the unraveling of democracy in contemporary times is made more complicated by technological innovation and the revolution in telecommunication . The emergence of new technologies , digital dynamics and the new media have raised the challenges of the relationship @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ At the core of this challenge is the dynamics of the social media increasing dominant influence in shaping knowledge formation in society and the citizens expectations from governments in the information age . Or more precisely , social media serves as the mechanism that fuels the danger of post-truth -- a contemporary manifestation where facts are manipulated in ways that undermine reason and promotes sentimental biases and political prejudices , especially in public opinion . At a most critical level , the social media constitutes a most fundamental mechanism by which the government , its apparatuses and the citizenry can facilitate and strengthen strategic communication that could consolidate democratic governance . Today , it is easy for the citizens to react in real time to government 's policies and decisions on issues that affect them . It is also easier for the government to reach the citizens and provide justifications for matters of state . Indeed , in an effort to modernize its governance processes , many governments across the world have deployed digital technologies and the social media to sign on to the open government initiative that is predicated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ processes of policies to the citizens . This has gone a long way not only to open up the working of bureaucratic structures and processes to the democratic scrutiny of the citizens , but has also made governments more legitimate in the eyes of their citizens . <p> However , the dynamics of information on social media is not as seamless as I have presented above . To the extent that information is crucial both for the dynamics of service delivery to the citizens and the management of democratic communication , the social media serves a most fundamental purpose that sustains political and democratic stability . Unfortunately , the social media is a double-edged sword . It cuts at the idea of the public good both ways , negatively and positively . At its best , social media offers the space and opportunity for the continuing adjustment of the social contract that promises betterment for all citizens . At its worst , it demonstrates the most terrible features of mass hysteria , especially in terms of lack of understanding and reflection on government policies and processes . <p> Indeed , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the deployment of information to navigate the perils of authoritarian government . Claude Shannon , the American mathematician , insists that " information is the resolution of uncertainty . " And he is right . However , information is power to the extent that it can be manipulated and distorted to suit purposes and objectives that are less than wholesome in political and bureaucratic terms . This is the essence of fake news ; the dynamics of misinformation and disinformation . This is exactly the message Edward de Bono , the Maltese physician , was trying to convey : " There 's a danger in the internet and social media . The notion that information is enough , that more and more information is enough , that you do n't have to think , you just have to get more information -- the more it gets very dangerous . " While misinformation is getting the facts wrong , disinformation is an act arising from a deliberate distortion of the facts . <p> How does the social media and the danger of disinformation work within a postcolonial context of democratic governance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ question that links the social media and its utility to the larger issues of nation-building , development administration and governance . A democratic government does not want to be perceived as being favorable to one ethnic or religious groups over the others . In other word , the bureaucracy is supposed to act as the mechanism by which the government reach all ethnic constituencies with the dividends of goof governance . <p> Disinformation erodes the capacity of Nigerians to relate with the bureaucracy as an apparatus that is unbiased and efficient .
